title: Monad
body:
The hub note of the second half of the course. A monad is a [[Type Class]] with two operations
that together let you **sequence computations that carry a context**, where each step may depend
on the value the previous step produced.

```haskell
class Applicative m => Monad m where
    return :: a -> m a                     -- put a plain value in, doing nothing else
    (>>=)  :: m a -> (a -> m b) -> m b     -- "bind": feed the result onward
```

`>>=` is the whole thing. It takes a value in a context, and a function that takes a *plain*
value and returns a *new* value in a context, and joins the two levels back into one. That
joining is the work: without it, chaining two `Maybe`-returning functions gives you
`Maybe (Maybe Int)` and you unwrap by hand forever.

## Why it exists: the staircase

Start from the problem, not the definition. Three lookups that may each fail:

```haskell
-- by hand
case lookup "user" env of
  Nothing -> Nothing
  Just u  -> case lookup "host" u of
    Nothing -> Nothing
    Just h  -> case lookup "port" h of
      Nothing -> Nothing
      Just p  -> Just (p + 1)
```

Every level is the same two lines of plumbing. Factor them out once:

```haskell
instance Monad Maybe where
    return x       = Just x
    Nothing >>= _  = Nothing        -- the entire failure story, written once
    Just x  >>= f  = f x
```

and the staircase collapses:

```haskell
lookup "user" env >>= lookup "host" >>= lookup "port" >>= \p -> return (p + 1)
```

`do` notation is sugar for exactly that chain, nothing more:

```haskell
do u <- lookup "user" env       -- x <- e  desugars to  e >>= \x ->
   h <- lookup "host" u
   p <- lookup "port" h
   return (p + 1)
```

The imperative look of `do` blocks is the joke at the centre of the language: it reads as
statements and it is a chain of function applications. Note that `<-` is the same arrow as
[[List Comprehension]]'s generator, for the same reason.

## The context differs, the shape does not

The point is that one interface covers unrelated plumbing:

| Monad | The context | `>>=` handles |
|---|---|---|
| `Maybe` | may be absent | short-circuiting on `Nothing` |
| `Either e` | may have failed with a reason | short-circuiting, carrying the error |
| `[]` (list) | many possible results | trying every combination: `concatMap` |
| `State s` | threads a value through | passing the updated state along |
| `IO` | performs a real effect | ordering the effects. See [[Monadic IO]] |

The list row is the one this course leans on twice. `xs >>= f` is `concatMap f xs`, so `return
x = [x]` is one result and `[]` is failure, and the whole of [[Recursive Backtracking]] is that
monad. It is also the executable version of [[Nondeterminism]]'s explore-all-branches reading,
which is the bridge back to [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]].

## The three laws

An instance is a monad only if it satisfies these, and they say `return` is a neutral element
and that grouping does not matter:

| Law | Statement |
|---|---|
| Left identity | `return a >>= f` $=$ `f a` |
| Right identity | `m >>= return` $=$ `m` |
| Associativity | `(m >>= f) >>= g` $=$ `m >>= (\x -> f x >>= g)` |

Not compiler-checked. Break them and `do` notation quietly stops meaning what it reads as: with
associativity broken, refactoring three lines of a `do` block into a helper changes the
program's behaviour. The pattern "an identity element plus associativity" is the monoid axioms
from [[Abstract Algebra]] (a [[Group]] without inverses), which is where the notorious "a monad
is a monoid in the category of endofunctors" comes from. See [[Category Theory]], where that
sentence is unpacked rather than quoted.

## What it is not

- **Not about IO.** `IO` is one instance of many, and `Maybe` is the one to learn on.
- **Not a design pattern you apply.** It is a property an existing type either has or does not.
- **Not impure.** `>>=` is a [[Pure Function]] and building an `IO` action performs nothing.
- **Not a container.** `State` and `IO` hold nothing; "wrapped value" is a useful lie that
  `Maybe` and `[]` support and the others do not.

## Core Facts to Know

- Two operations: `return :: a -> m a` and `>>= :: m a -> (a -> m b) -> m b`.
- `>>=` sequences computations in a context, flattening the two levels it would otherwise make.
- Its power over `Applicative`: the next step may **depend on** the previous step's value.
- `do` notation is pure sugar; `x <- e` is `e >>= \x ->`.
- Every monad is an `Applicative`, and every applicative is a [[Functor]].
- `Maybe` short-circuits on `Nothing`, so the null check is written once in the instance.
- The list monad's `>>=` is `concatMap`; it is [[Recursive Backtracking]] and [[Nondeterminism]].
- Three laws: left identity, right identity, associativity. Not checked by the compiler.
- Associativity is what makes refactoring a `do` block safe.
- Identity plus associativity is the monoid shape from [[Abstract Algebra]].
